task_statement:
Research question (as posed on 2026-11-01, in the area of player absence and offensive reorganization):
The teammate with the closest pre-absence initiation profile (or most minutes / initiations / same-position minutes) is the largest gainer in the absent player's primary types.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.
- Units available to a study of this question (as recorded): n=148; 148 spells; 11 cases

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

historical_evidence.finding: Play-type replacement similarity does not separate absorption from cascade; mean similarity ABSORBED +0.863 vs CASCADE +0.848, Spearman rank correlation (sim, -gap) = -0.19 (wrong-signed). Embiid 23-24 cascades with Reed sim 0.94. Verdict: null (adequately powered null).
Within-game did_adapt toward SHOULD counters improves PPP; adapters +0.0701 vs non-adapters +0.0121 PPP, but limited by selection/regression to the mean.

Travel x fit screen vs real player outcomes (minutes, usage, net rating); net-rating gap between additive and irrelevant is large but correlation with delta is low (+0.077), fit_score correlations negative. n=198 movers.

A1 within-scheme re-test controlling early-third PPP selection; within-scheme gaps DROP +0.0830 (p=0.0046), HELP +0.0539 (p=0.0493), SWITCH -0.0199 (p=0.6514); carryover not significant. Mechanism unclear.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Using teammate initiation profile similarity to predict whether a player's absence leads to absorption or cascade in play types.
failed_approaches.why: Similarity scores are almost always high and do not separate outcomes; Spearman correlation with gap is wrong-signed. Adequately powered null result.

evidence_establishes: Teammate play-type initiation profile similarity, as previously measured, does not separate the two main organizational outcomes (absorption vs cascade) when a player sits.
High similarity is near-universal and therefore lacks discriminative power for identifying the primary beneficiary of an absence.
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether alternative proximity measures (most minutes, most initiations, same-position minutes) would predict the largest gainer in the absent player's primary types.
Whether any metric can outperform a simple minutes-based allocation in predicting which teammate gains most in specific play types.
Why similarity fails (e.g., label error, defensive versus offensive profile mismatch, or insufficient variance).
Results in larger or more targeted samples, as the prior study used approximately 23 absences with unrecorded power.
own_inferences: The current question is a variant of the null hypothesis already tested: the closest-profile teammate is the biggest gainer. The prior null result makes support unlikely.
The available data records only 11 cases, which is insufficient for a correlation or rank-based test with usable statistical power.
Using minutes or same-position minutes may be more predictive than profile similarity, but this is speculative and would still suffer from severe sample size constraints.
Confounders such as coaching decisions, opponent adjustments, and regression to the mean in play-type shares are unresolved and likely to bias any naive analysis.
uncertainties: Why the system reports n=148 spells but only 11 cases; the definition of a usable case for this hypothesis is unclear.
How 'primary types' of the absent player are defined and whether they remain stable during absence.
How much variance in teammate gain is actually expected after accounting for simple opportunity measures.
The exact similarity metric used in the prior study and whether it can be improved.

historical_effect.explanation: The prior finding that initiation-profile similarity is almost always high and does not separate absorption from cascade indicates the core premise of the hypothesis is likely false. Without that evidence, one might have considered the question testable; with it, the probability of a meaningful result is very low, especially given only 11 cases.

blocking_constraints.text: Only 11 cases available; any test of correlation between a similarity metric and gain would be severely underpowered.
Few absence spells where a single replacement can be clearly identified; most absences involve committee adjustments.
Primary play types and gain must be derived from play-by-play data; classification errors may swamp the signal.

prior_work.summary: SF-[prior work] directly tested the hypothesis that a similar-profile teammate separates absorption from cascade and obtained an adequately powered null result. The current question is a refinement of that hypothesis (largest gainer in primary types), but the underlying logic is the same, and the prior null strongly suggests this refinement will also fail.

risks.text: 11 cases would require an extremely large effect size to reach 80% power; typical effect sizes in these settings are small.
Defining primary types and gain requires arbitrary thresholds; classification error can create or obscure relationships.
Coaching decisions, opponent defensive schemes, and the health of other teammates influence who gains, not just profile similarity.
Players with extreme pre-absence usage may see natural regression after an absence, conflating gain estimates.
Testing multiple similarity metrics (profile, minutes, initiations, same-position) without adjustment increases false positive risk.

design.estimand: Correlation between teammate rank by pre-absence similarity (or minutes[path] minutes) and their rank by post-absence change in share of the absent player's primary play types, among eligible replacements.
design.sample: All absence spells where (a) the absent player missed games due to injury/rest, (b) at least 3 games pre- and post-absence data for the team, and (c) at least two teammates saw minutes in the absent player's primary types. Estimated n≈11.
design.power: A two-sided Spearman rank correlation test with n=11 would require a true ρ ≈ 0.75 to achieve 80% power; such a large effect is implausible given the prior null of ρ ≈ –0.19 qualitatively. Therefore minimum viable power is unachievable.
design.controls: None feasible with this sample size; covariates would further reduce degrees of freedom. A best-practices design would match on expected minutes bump, pre-absence usage, and position.
design.falsification: Test whether the similarity metric predicts gain in secondary (non-primary) types; a similar coefficient there would indicate the measure captures general opportunity, not specific replacement effects. Negative control: look at teammates with the least similarity and confirm they are never the largest gainers.
design.multiplicity: All similarity criteria would need Bonferroni correction; with three metrics and 11 cases, adjusted α would render any result non-significant.
design.decision_rule: Reject the null of no correlation if the Spearman ρ for the pre-specified primary metric exceeds the critical value at α=0.05/3. Given power <10%, any null result is uninformative; thus the test cannot produce a useful conclusion.
design.data_version: NBA 2022-23 through 2025-26 regular season and playoffs, play-by-play and derived play-type records, as of 2026-11-01.
